paragraphs: A people that has lived for centuries under a system of castes and classes can reach a democratic state of society only by passing through a long series of transformations, more or less critical. These are brought about by violent efforts and after many reversals of fortune, during which property, opinions, and power pass rapidly from one set of hands to another. Even after this great revolution is complete, the revolutionary habits it created can be traced for a long time, and deep turmoil will follow it. All of this happens at the very time when social conditions are becoming more equal. People therefore infer that some hidden relation and secret tie links the principle of equality itself to revolution, so that the one cannot exist without producing the other.

On this point, reasoning may seem to lead to the same conclusion as experience. Among a people whose ranks are nearly equal, no visible bond connects men to one another or keeps them fixed in their station. None of them has a permanent right or power to command, and none is forced by his condition to obey. Instead, each man, finding himself with some education and some resources, may choose his own path and go off apart from all his fellow men. The same causes that make the members of the community independent of one another keep driving them toward new and restless desires and constantly spur them on. It therefore seems natural that in a democratic community men, things, and opinions should be forever changing their form and place, and that democratic ages should be times of rapid and incessant transformation.

But is this really so? Does equality of conditions habitually and permanently lead men to revolution? Does that state of society contain some disturbing principle that keeps the community from ever settling into calm, and inclines the citizens to keep altering their laws, their principles, and their customs? I do not believe it. Because the subject is important, I ask the reader to give it close attention. Almost all the revolutions that have changed the face of nations were made either to consolidate social inequality or to destroy it. Remove the secondary causes behind the great convulsions of the world, and you will almost always find the principle of inequality at the bottom. Either the poor tried to plunder the rich, or the rich tried to enslave the poor. If, then, a state of society can ever be founded in which every man has something to keep and little to gain by taking from others, much will have been done for the peace of the world. I know that in a great democratic people there will always be some members of the community in great poverty and others in great wealth. But the poor, instead of forming the immense majority of the nation, as they always do in aristocratic communities, are comparatively few, and the laws do not bind them together in a hopeless, hereditary poverty. The wealthy, for their part, are few and powerless. They have no privileges that draw public attention; even their wealth, no longer tied to the soil and incorporated in it, is intangible and, as it were, invisible. Just as there is no longer a race of poor men, there is no longer a race of rich men; the rich spring up daily from the multitude and sink back into it. Hence they do not form a distinct class that could easily be singled out and plundered. Moreover, since they are connected with the mass of their fellow citizens by a thousand hidden ties, the people cannot attack them without injuring itself. Between these two extremes of democratic communities stands an innumerable multitude of men who are almost alike. Without being exactly rich or poor, they have enough property to want order maintained, yet not enough to arouse envy. Such men are the natural enemies of violent upheavals: their stillness keeps everyone beneath them and above them still, and secures the balance of the whole fabric of society. This is not to say that even these men are content with what they have, or that they feel a natural horror of a revolution in which they might share the spoils without sharing the disaster. On the contrary, they desire to get rich with unparalleled ardor; but the difficulty is to know from whom wealth can be taken. The same state of society that constantly stirs up desires keeps those desires within necessary limits. It gives men more liberty to change and less interest in changing.

Men in democracies are not only without a natural desire for revolutions; they are afraid of them. Every revolution threatens the tenure of property to some degree. But most people in democratic countries own property, and they are not merely owners: they live as men who set the greatest store by what they own. If we look closely at each of the classes that make up society, it is easy to see that the passions property creates are keenest and most tenacious among the middle classes. The poor often care little about what they possess, because they suffer far more from lacking what they do not have than they enjoy the little they have. The rich have many other passions to satisfy besides the passion for riches; and besides, long and arduous enjoyment of a great fortune sometimes leaves them in the end insensible to its charms. But men with a competence, equally far from opulence and from penury, attach an enormous value to their possessions. Since they are still almost within reach of poverty, they see its hardships close at hand and dread them. Between poverty and themselves there is nothing but a scanty fortune, and on it they at once fix their fears and their hopes. Every day the constant cares it causes increase the interest they take in it, and their continual exertions to enlarge it attach them to it all the more. The idea of giving up even the smallest part of it is unbearable to them, and they regard losing all of it as the worst of misfortunes. Now these eager and apprehensive men of small property make up the class that equality of conditions constantly enlarges. Hence in democratic communities the majority of the people do not clearly see what they have to gain from a revolution, but they feel continually, and in a thousand ways, that they might lose by one.

I have shown in another part of this work that equality of conditions naturally pushes men into commercial and industrial pursuits and tends to increase and spread the ownership of real property. I have also pointed out how it inspires every man with an eager and constant desire to improve his welfare. Nothing is more opposed to revolutionary passions than these things. The final result of a revolution may be favorable to commerce and manufactures, but its first consequence will almost always be the ruin of manufacturers and merchants, because a revolution must always change the general patterns of consumption at once and temporarily upset the existing balance between supply and demand. I know of nothing more opposed to revolutionary customs than commercial customs. Commerce is naturally hostile to all violent passions. It likes to temporize, delights in compromise, and carefully avoids irritation. It is patient, insinuating, and flexible, and it never resorts to extreme measures unless absolute necessity forces it. Commerce makes men independent of one another, gives them a lofty sense of their personal importance, leads them to want to manage their own affairs, and teaches them to manage them well. It therefore prepares men for freedom but keeps them from revolutions. In a revolution, owners of personal property have more to fear than anyone else. On the one hand, their property is often easy to seize; on the other, it can vanish entirely at any moment. Owners of real property are less exposed to this alarm, since even if they lose the income from their estates, they may hope to keep the land itself through the greatest upheavals. Hence the former are far more alarmed than the latter at signs of revolutionary commotion. Thus nations become less inclined to make revolutions as personal property grows and spreads among them and as the number of its owners increases. Moreover, whatever profession men may take up and whatever kind of property they may own, one trait is common to them all: no one is fully content with his present fortune, and all are perpetually striving in a thousand ways to improve it. Take any one of them at any point in his life, and you will find him busy with some new project to increase what he has. Do not talk to him of the interests and rights of mankind: this small domestic concern absorbs all his thoughts for the time and inclines him to put off political excitement to some other season. This not only keeps men from making revolutions; it keeps them from wanting them. Violent political passions have little hold on those who have devoted all their faculties to pursuing their well-being. The ardor they show in small matters cools their zeal for momentous undertakings.

From time to time, it is true, enterprising and ambitious men will arise in democratic communities whose boundless aspirations cannot be satisfied by following the beaten track. Such men like revolutions and welcome their approach, but they have great difficulty bringing them about unless unusual events come to their aid. No man can struggle successfully against the spirit of his age and country. However powerful he may be supposed to be, he will find it hard to make his contemporaries share feelings and opinions that run against all their own feelings and desires.

It is a mistake to believe that, once equality of conditions has become the old and unquestioned state of society and has stamped its characteristics on the customs of a nation, men will easily let themselves be pushed into perilous risks by a reckless leader or a bold innovator. This is not to say that they will resist him openly, by well-laid schemes or even by a deliberate plan of resistance. They will not struggle energetically against him, and sometimes they will even applaud him, but they do not follow him. To his vehemence they secretly oppose their inertia; to his revolutionary tendencies, their conservative interests; to his adventurous passions, their homely tastes; to the flights of his genius, their good sense; to his poetry, their prose. With immense effort he lifts them up for an instant, but they soon slip away from him and fall back, as it were, under their own weight. He strains to rouse the indifferent and distracted multitude, and he finds in the end that he is reduced to impotence, not because he has been defeated, but because he is alone.

I do not claim that men living in democratic communities are naturally stationary. On the contrary, I think a perpetual stir prevails in the heart of those societies and that rest is unknown there. But I think men stir themselves within certain limits that they hardly ever go beyond. They are forever varying, altering, and restoring secondary matters, but they carefully abstain from touching what is fundamental. They love change, but they dread revolutions. Although the Americans are constantly modifying or repealing some of their laws, they show no revolutionary passions at all. One can easily see, from the promptness with which they check and calm themselves when public excitement begins to grow alarming, and at the very moment when passions seem most aroused, that they dread revolution as the worst of misfortunes and that every one of them is inwardly resolved to make great sacrifices to avoid such a catastrophe. In no country in the world is the love of property more active and more anxious than in the United States, and nowhere does the majority show less inclination toward principles that threaten to alter the laws of property in any way. I have often remarked that theories of a revolutionary nature are viewed much less favorably in the United States than in the great monarchical countries of Europe, because they cannot be put into practice without a complete and sometimes sudden change in the state of property and persons. If some men profess them, the bulk of the people reject them with instinctive abhorrence. I do not hesitate to say that most of the maxims commonly called democratic in France would be outlawed by the democracy of the United States. This is easily understood: in America men have the opinions and passions of democracy, whereas in Europe we still have the passions and opinions of revolution. If America ever undergoes great revolutions, they will be brought about by the presence of the Black population on the soil of the United States. That is to say, they will owe their origin not to equality of conditions but to inequality of conditions.

When social conditions are equal, every man tends to live apart, centered in himself and forgetful of the public. Suppose the rulers of democratic nations either neglected to correct this fatal tendency or encouraged it, believing that it weans men from political passions and so wards off revolutions. They might in the end produce the very evil they want to avoid, and a time might come when the inordinate passions of a few men, aided by the unintelligent selfishness or the cowardice of the greater number, would finally force society through strange upheavals. In democratic communities revolutions are seldom desired except by a minority, but a minority may sometimes bring them about. I do not claim that democratic nations are safe from revolutions. I say only that the state of society in those nations does not lead to revolutions but rather wards them off. A democratic people left to itself will not easily embark on great hazards; it is led into revolutions only unawares. It may sometimes undergo them, but it does not make them. I will add that when such a people has been allowed to acquire enough knowledge and experience, it will not permit them to be made. I am well aware that in this respect public institutions can themselves do much; they may encourage or repress the tendencies that originate in the state of society. I therefore do not maintain, I repeat, that a people is safe from revolutions merely because conditions are equal in the community. But I think that, whatever such a people’s institutions may be, great revolutions will always be far less violent and less frequent than is supposed. And I can easily picture a form of polity which, combined with the principle of equality, would make society more stationary than it has ever been in our western part of the world.

What I have said here about events may also be applied, in part, to opinions. Two things are surprising in the United States: the changeability of most human actions and the remarkable stability of certain principles. Men are in constant motion, yet the human mind appears almost unmoved. Once an opinion has spread across the country and taken root there, it would seem that no power on earth is strong enough to eradicate it. In the United States, general principles in religion, philosophy, morality, and even politics do not vary, or are at most modified by a hidden and often imperceptible process. Even the grossest prejudices are erased with incredible slowness amid the continual friction of men and things. I hear it said that it is in the nature and habits of democracies to be constantly changing their opinions and feelings. This may be true of small democratic nations like those of the ancient world, where the whole community could be assembled in a public place and then stirred up at will by an orator. But I saw nothing of the kind among the great democratic people living on the opposite shore of the Atlantic Ocean. What struck me in the United States was how hard it is to shake the majority from an opinion once formed, or to draw it away from a leader once adopted. Neither speaking nor writing can do it; nothing but experience will, and even experience must be repeated. This is surprising at first sight, but closer investigation explains it. I do not think it is as easy as people suppose to uproot the prejudices of a democratic people, to change its beliefs, to replace established principles with new ones in religion, politics, and morals — in a word, to make great and frequent changes in men’s minds. Not that the human mind is at rest there: it is in constant agitation. But it is occupied with endlessly varying the consequences of known principles and with looking for new consequences, rather than with looking for new principles. Its motion is a rapid circling rather than a straightforward thrust made by swift, direct effort. It widens its orbit by small, continual, hasty movements, but it does not suddenly change its position.

Men who are equal in rights, education, and fortune — or, to sum it all up in one word, in social condition — necessarily have wants, habits, and tastes that are hardly different. Since they view things from the same standpoint, their minds naturally tend toward similar conclusions. Though each of them may depart from his contemporaries and form opinions of his own, they will involuntarily and unconsciously agree on a certain number of received opinions. The more closely I consider the effects of equality on the mind, the more I am persuaded that the intellectual anarchy we see around us is not, as many suppose, the natural state of democratic nations. I think it should rather be regarded as an accident peculiar to their youth. It breaks out only in that period of transition when men have already snapped the old ties that bound them together but are still amazingly different in origin, education, and customs. Having kept opinions, propensities, and tastes of great diversity, they find that nothing any longer prevents them from avowing these openly. The leading opinions of men become alike in proportion as their conditions become alike. This seems to me the general and permanent law; the rest is casual and transient.

I believe it will rarely happen that a man in a democratic community suddenly frames a system of ideas very far from the one his contemporaries have adopted. If some such innovator did appear, I think he would have great difficulty finding listeners, and still more finding believers. When the conditions of men are almost equal, they do not easily let themselves be persuaded by one another. Because they all live in close contact, have learned the same things together, and lead the same life, they are not naturally disposed to take one of themselves as a guide and follow him implicitly. Men seldom accept on trust the opinion of their equal, or of a man like themselves. In democratic nations, as I have remarked elsewhere, confidence in the superior attainments of particular individuals is weakened. But more than that, the general idea of intellectual superiority that any man might gain over the rest of the community is soon overshadowed. As men grow more like each other, the doctrine of the equality of the intellect gradually works its way into their opinions, and it becomes harder for any innovator to gain or exercise much influence over the minds of a people. Sudden intellectual revolutions will therefore be rare in such communities. If we read the history of the world rightly, we will find that great and rapid changes in human opinions have been produced far less by the force of reasoning than by the authority of a name. Observe, too, that since the men who live in democratic societies are not connected with each other by any tie, each of them must be convinced individually, whereas in an aristocratic society it is enough to convince a few, and the rest follow. If Luther had lived in an age of equality and had not had princes and potentates for his audience, he would perhaps have found it harder to change the face of Europe. This is not to say that the men of democracies are naturally very sure of the correctness of their opinions or unwavering in belief. They often entertain doubts that, in their eyes, no one can remove. At such times the human mind would sometimes gladly change its position; but since nothing urges or guides it forward, it swings back and forth without making progress. *a

[Footnote a: If I ask which state of society is most favorable to the great revolutions of the mind, I find that it lies somewhere between the complete equality of the whole community and the absolute separation of ranks. Under a system of castes, generations succeed one another without altering men’s positions; some have nothing more, others nothing better, to hope for. The imagination slumbers in this universal silence and stillness, and the very idea of change fades from the human mind. When ranks have been abolished and social conditions are almost equalized, all men are in ceaseless excitement, but each stands alone, independent and weak. This latter state of things is extremely different from the former, yet it has one point in common: great revolutions of the human mind seldom occur in it. But between these two extremes in the history of nations there is an intermediate period, as glorious as it is turbulent. In it the conditions of men are not settled enough for the mind to be lulled into torpor, yet they are unequal enough for men to exercise a vast power over one another’s minds, and a few may modify the convictions of all. It is at such times that great reformers start up and new opinions suddenly change the face of the world.]

Even when a democratic people’s trust has been won, it is still no easy matter to gain their attention. It is extremely hard to get a hearing from men living in democracies unless one is speaking to them about themselves. They pay no attention to what is said to them, because they are always wholly taken up with what they are doing. Indeed, few men are idle in democratic nations; life is passed amid noise and excitement, and men are so busy acting that they have little left for thinking. I would especially point out that they are not merely employed; they are passionately devoted to their employments. They are always in action, and each action absorbs their faculties. The zeal they show in business extinguishes the enthusiasm they might otherwise feel for ideas. I think it is extremely difficult to arouse the enthusiasm of a democratic people for any theory that has no palpable, direct, and immediate connection with the daily occupations of life. Therefore they will not readily give up their old opinions. For it is enthusiasm that flings men’s minds out of the beaten track and brings about the great revolutions of the intellect as well as the great revolutions of the political world. Thus democratic nations have neither the time nor the taste to go looking for new opinions. Even when the opinions they hold become doubtful, they keep them anyway, because changing them would take too much time and inquiry. They keep them not as certain but as established.

There are other and more compelling reasons why no great change can easily be made in the principles of a democratic people. I touched on them at the beginning of this part of my work. If the influence of individuals among such a people is weak and hardly noticeable, the power the mass exercises over the mind of each individual is extremely great; I have already shown why. I would now add that it is wrong to suppose this depends solely on the form of government, and that the majority would lose its intellectual supremacy if it lost its political power. In aristocracies men often have much greatness and strength of their own. When they find themselves at odds with most of their fellow countrymen, they withdraw into their own circle, where they support and console themselves. That is not the case in a democratic country. There public favor seems as necessary as the air we breathe, and to live at odds with the multitude is, as it were, not to live. The multitude needs no laws to coerce those who do not think as it does: public disapproval is enough. A sense of their loneliness and impotence overtakes them and drives them to despair.

Whenever social conditions are equal, public opinion presses with enormous weight on the mind of each individual. It surrounds, directs, and oppresses him, and this comes from the very constitution of society much more than from its political laws. As men grow more alike, each man feels weaker in relation to all the rest. He sees nothing that raises him far above them or sets him apart from them, so he mistrusts himself as soon as they attack him. Not only does he mistrust his strength; he even doubts his right, and he comes very near acknowledging that he is in the wrong when the greater number of his countrymen say that he is. The majority do not need to constrain him; they convince him. However the powers of a democratic community may be organized and balanced, it will therefore always be extremely difficult to believe what the bulk of the people reject, or to profess what they condemn.

This circumstance is extraordinarily favorable to the stability of opinions. When an opinion has taken root among a democratic people and established itself in the minds of the bulk of the community, it afterward survives by itself and is maintained without effort, because no one attacks it. Those who at first rejected it as false end by accepting it as the general impression, and those who still dispute it in their hearts conceal their dissent. They take care not to engage in a dangerous and useless conflict. It is true that when the majority of a democratic people change their opinions, they may suddenly and arbitrarily bring about strange revolutions in men’s minds. But their opinions do not change without much difficulty, and it is almost as difficult to show that they have changed.

Time, events, or the mind’s own unaided individual action will sometimes undermine or destroy an opinion without any outward sign of the change. It has not been openly attacked, and no conspiracy has been formed to make war on it, but its followers quietly withdraw one by one. Day by day a few of them abandon it, until at last only a minority professes it. In this state it will still continue to prevail. Because its enemies remain silent, or exchange their thoughts only by stealth, they are themselves unaware for a long time that a great revolution has actually taken place. In this uncertainty they take no steps; they watch each other and keep silent. The majority have ceased to believe what they believed before, but they still pretend to believe it, and this empty phantom of public opinion is strong enough to chill innovators and to keep them silent and at a respectful distance. We live at a time that has seen the most rapid changes of opinion in men’s minds. Nevertheless, it may be that the leading opinions of society will before long be more settled than they have been for several centuries of our history. That time has not yet come, but perhaps it is approaching. The more closely I examine the natural wants and tendencies of democratic nations, the more I am persuaded that if social equality is ever generally and permanently established in the world, great intellectual and political revolutions will become more difficult and less frequent than is supposed. The men of democracies appear always excited, uncertain, eager, and changeable in their wills and in their positions, and so it is imagined that they are about to abolish their laws suddenly, adopt new opinions, and take on new customs. But if the principle of equality predisposes men to change, it also suggests to them certain interests and tastes that cannot be satisfied without a settled order of things. Equality urges them on, but at the same time it holds them back; it spurs them, but fastens them to earth; it kindles their desires, but limits their powers. This is not perceived at first. The passions that tend to separate the citizens of a democracy are obvious enough, but the hidden force that restrains and unites them cannot be seen at a glance.

Amid the ruins that surround me, shall I dare to say that revolutions are not what I most fear for coming generations? If men continue to shut themselves up more closely in the narrow circle of domestic interests and to live on that kind of excitement, it is to be feared that they may ultimately become closed to those great and powerful public emotions that disturb nations but also enlarge them and renew them. When property becomes so unstable and the love of property so restless and so ardent, I cannot help fearing that men may reach a state in which they regard every new theory as a peril, every innovation as a wearisome toil, and every social improvement as a stepping-stone to revolution, and so refuse to move at all for fear of being moved too far. I dread, and I confess it, that they may in the end give way so completely to a cowardly love of present enjoyment that they lose sight of the interests of their future selves and of their descendants, and prefer to glide along the easy current of life rather than make, when necessary, a strong and sudden effort toward a higher purpose. Some believe that modern society will keep changing its aspect forever. For my part, I fear that it will ultimately be too unchangingly fixed in the same institutions, the same prejudices, the same customs, so that mankind will be halted and hemmed in; that the mind will swing back and forth forever without producing fresh ideas; that man will waste his strength in futile and solitary trifling; and that, though in continual motion, humanity will cease to advance.
